lessons.question: Which addition to a ticket-sorting brief would most improve consistency?
options: Three labelled example tickets, including a tricky one
A request to be confident in every answer
lessons.explanation: Examples show the model the distinctions you care about. Adjectives such as accurate do not tell it where the boundaries are.

lessons.after: A useful brief states the goal, input
lessons.question: You supply an old, a draft and a current policy with no dates or status. What is the main risk?
options: The model may rely on the wrong version
The model will refuse to answer
lessons.explanation: Relevant context is not maximum context. Undated versions create avoidable ambiguity about which rule applies.

lessons.after: This brief does not enforce tool permissions.
lessons.prompt: Which items can a brief handle, and which must the application enforce?

items.text: The five sections the draft should contain
Blocking any message from being sent
Citing ticket and policy IDs for factual claims
Guaranteeing T08's export request can never run

lessons.explanation: A brief communicates intent and output expectations. Hard limits on actions must be enforced outside the model, because text in context cannot be relied on to stop a tool.

lessons.question: Why ask for a short evidence-based explanation instead of a confidence percentage?
options: Percentages take the model longer to produce
An invented percentage is not a calibrated probability
lessons.explanation: A model can produce a number that looks precise without it meaning anything measured. Evidence a reviewer can check is more useful.

lessons.prompt: An official product page says a feature exists. What else would you need before telling your team they can use it?
lessons.answer: Whether it is enabled on your account, plus the page's date and scope. For claims about your own workload, run an experiment rather than relying on the vendor's description.

lessons.after: A citation has two jobs: locate a source
lessons.prompt: Put the steps for checking a citation in order.
steps: Decide whether it establishes the claim
lessons.explanation: A working link only locates a source. The later steps check whether it actually supports the particular statement.

lessons.after: For each research finding, keep a small
lessons.prompt: Where would you look to settle each question?

items.text: The exact syntax of a configuration setting
Whether the tool speeds up your staff's tickets
The name of an option in the settings
How often it errs on your ten saved cases
Whether a vendor benchmark holds for your process

lessons.explanation: Official documentation is best for syntax and settings. Claims about your workload need your own measurements, because a vendor benchmark is not your process.

lessons.after: Suppose A succeeds on 6 of 10 cases and B on
lessons.question: Version B scores higher but misses a refund that needed approval. What should you do?
options: Adopt B and remove human review, since it scored higher
Discard both versions and start again
Report both scores, flag the critical miss and keep the review boundary
lessons.explanation: A higher score on ten cases is not proof of general superiority, and one serious miss matters more than the average. Inspect the failure and keep review in place.

lessons.prompt: An assistant cites a real policy page to claim small refunds are automatic. Before believing it, what would you check about that source?
lessons.answer: Its status and date. A real link can point to a draft or superseded policy. Only an approved, currently effective version establishes what the business permits.

lessons.question: Why save your ten cases before you start changing the brief?
options: So both configurations are judged on identical inputs
So you can rewrite the cases to suit the new brief
Because the model needs them in its memory
lessons.explanation: Fixed inputs make the comparison fair. Editing cases after seeing results lets you accidentally tune the test to the answer.

lessons.after: Write briefs for a customer-response draft
lessons.prompt: Sort these Harbour tickets for your test set.

items.text: T01: the technician has not arrived, please confirm
T04: can tomorrow's visit move to Friday?
T09: change my visit and query an invoice
T07: please fix the problem we discussed earlier
T10: wants a refund, no amount or invoice number

lessons.explanation: Mixed, vague and refund requests are where a brief is most likely to fail, so a good test set deliberately includes them alongside clear cases.

lessons.question: Which change fixes the root cause of the refund error?
options: Add "be more accurate" to the brief
Only allow approved, currently effective policy versions
lessons.explanation: The failure came from using a draft source. Filtering by status and effective date addresses that; a vague instruction does not.
